title: Seventh commandment (CCC 2401–2449)
hook: don't steal, pay fair wages, share the earth's goods

segments.voice: Yesterday, chastity: the person whole, body and spirit in tune, no double life. Your line was whole, not divided. Where did you close the gap by one step? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

In the back of a garage, behind the bikes, leans a ladder. It belongs to the neighbor. It was borrowed for one gutter job, a few summers ago, and it has quietly become part of the furniture. Nobody would call it stealing. Nobody would call it giving back, either. In Jericho, a rich tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus pass, and before the day is over he's promising to pay back fourfold anyone he has cheated. The seventh commandment reaches from the ladder to the tax office.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER IN THE GARAGE.` → `A TAX COLLECTOR IN A TREE.` → `PAYING IT BACK.`

segments.voice: The commandment in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not steal." Four words, and the Catechism builds a whole picture of economic life on them. It starts not with property but with creation. In the beginning, it says, God entrusted the earth and its resources to the common stewardship of humanity. The goods of creation are meant for the whole human race. Private property is legitimate, the Catechism says: it secures freedom and dignity, and helps people meet their needs. But owning something doesn't cancel that first purpose. What a person owns is held for their family and also, in some way, for others. Then the Catechism names theft, and widens it. Not only taking what isn't yours, but keeping things lent or found. Fraud in business. Paying unjust wages. Raising prices by exploiting someone's ignorance or hardship. Work done poorly. Tax evasion. Waste. The ladder in the garage belongs on that list. And it asks for repair: what was taken should be given back. That's Zacchaeus in Luke's Gospel. He tells Jesus he'll give half his goods to the poor, and that if he has wronged anyone, he'll restore it fourfold. Jesus answers that salvation has come to that house. The Catechism goes on to wages. A just wage, it says, is the legitimate fruit of work, and refusing or withholding it can be a grave injustice. And it ends with love for the poor. It quotes Gregory the Great. In paraphrase: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't giving them what's ours, but returning what's theirs. Theft, in this commandment, isn't only a hand in someone's pocket. It's anything that keeps the earth's goods from reaching the people they were made for.
screen: `THE EARTH ENTRUSTED TO ALL.` · `THEFT, WIDENED.` · `ZACCHAEUS PAYS IT BACK.` · `FAIR WAGES, AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay or tip fairly today. Settle, and breathe. Think through the people whose work you'll use today: the driver, the server, the cashier, the cleaner, the person on the help line. Picture one of them clearly, their hands, their long shift. Decide now what fair looks like for them: a better tip, a prompt payment, a thank-you, a fair review. And if anything borrowed is still in your house, decide when it goes back. If you pray, you can ask for a generous hand. The bell holds the time.
Seventh commandment. Thou shalt not steal: respect for others' goods, fair wages, honest work, repair of what was taken, and the earth's goods shared with all, especially the poor. Today's word.
Your line: goods are for all. Today, pay or tip one person a little more fairly than you have to, and return one thing you've borrowed. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught to make restitution for what they've taken, to pay and work fairly, and to give to the poor through almsgiving, parish collections and the works of mercy.

match.prompt: the seventh commandment — tap the pairs.
pairs: meant for the whole human race
giving the poor what is theirs

myth: the seventh commandment is only about taking things
the Catechism also names keeping things lent, unjust wages, fraud, poor work and waste.
the Catechism calls it legitimate, while holding that the earth's goods are meant for all.
the Catechism asks for things taken to be given back
repair is part of the commandment, as Zacchaeus shows.

fork.setup: you're Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector. Jesus has just invited himself to your house, and the crowd is muttering. what do you do?
options: keep quiet and enjoy the dinner.
give half your goods to the poor, and repay anyone you cheated fourfold.
hand back the exact amount and no more.
fork.reveal: in Luke 19, Zacchaeus stands and promises half to the poor and fourfold repayment, and Jesus says salvation has come to that house.

trapdoor: what it means: respect others' goods, work and pay fairly, give back what was taken, and share the earth's goods.
what a scholar hears: the universal destination of goods, restitution after Zacchaeus, the just wage, and love for the poor.

sources.ref: Gregory the Great, Regula Pastoralis 3.21, quoted in CCC 2446

notes: CCC 2401–2449 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Universal destination and private property CCC 2402–2406; widened theft CCC 2409; reparation and Zacchaeus CCC 2412; just wage CCC 2434; love for the poor and Gregory the Great CCC 2443–2449.
'Four words' counts the Douay-Rheims 'Thou shalt not steal'; confirm.
Exodus 20:15 quoted from Douay-Rheims; the verse number may differ in some editions. Confirm.
Zacchaeus paraphrased from Luke 19:8–9; 'half his goods' and 'fourfold' are stated in the text.
Hook: 'before the day is over' follows Jesus' 'this day' in Luke 19:9.
Stewardship of creation (CCC 2415–2418) is left for tomorrow. Original set to null.
